reasons: No test file for this module is visible in the packet.
The header promises checks on numbers and web addresses that this function does not show.
Names that are also common words are deliberately exempt, which is a known gap.

terms.meaning: a named company, place or project
one word taken out of a longer text
a capital letter in the middle of a word, such as in a name written as two joined words
a piece of text that sits inside a longer text
the root form of a word with its endings removed

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose and rules of the guard
sections.what: Explains that the guard rejects company, place and project names that the model invented, and lists the cases where a word is let through without a check.
sections.why: The header says the earlier rule rejected ordinary words, so the rules were narrowed.
sections.watch_out: An entity whose name is also an ordinary English word is not checked, so a made-up name of that kind can pass.

sections.name: ENGLISH
sections.title: Large English word list
sections.what: Loads about 275,000 lower-case English words from a package. The guard uses this list to decide whether a word is ordinary English.
sections.why: The comment says this list is included to stop normal words from being flagged, while leaving out real company and place names.
sections.watch_out: Any word in this list is exempt from the check, so an updated package can change results.

sections.name: COMMON_WORDS (part 1)
sections.title: Everyday word list, first part
sections.what: Adds the guard's own list of common words: pronouns, conjunctions, verbs, and project and energy vocabulary that the large list lacks.
sections.why: The comment says this list adds domain words and function words without overriding the large list.
sections.watch_out: Any word added here is exempt from the check, so the list should hold only common words, never names.

sections.name: COMMON_WORDS (part 2)
sections.title: Everyday word list, second part
sections.what: Adds more everyday vocabulary: business terms, risks and delays, common adjectives and adverbs, and numbers and directions.
sections.why: The header says words like these were being wrongly rejected before, so they were added here.
sections.watch_out: A company whose name matches one of these words will pass the check.

sections.name: COMMON_WORDS (part 3)
sections.title: End of the word list
sections.what: Closes the everyday word list block.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: DERIVATIONAL_SUFFIXES
sections.title: Endings that mark ordinary words
sections.what: Lists word endings such as -ment, -tion, -ness, -ive and -ical that ordinary vocabulary uses and names rarely do. Words with these endings are exempt from the check.
sections.why: The comment says these endings are common in ordinary words but almost never in names. Plain -al is left out on purpose so that place names such as Portugal are still checked.
sections.watch_out: A real name that ends in one of these endings, such as a name ending in -ship, is exempt from the check.

sections.name: stripPlural
sections.title: Remove plural endings
sections.what: Turns a plural word into its singular form, for example removing s or es, or changing ies to y.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets plural forms match the word list and the source material.
sections.watch_out: The simple rules misread some words, such as news, which becomes new.

sections.name: inflectionBases
sections.title: Possible root forms of a word
sections.what: Produces possible root forms of a word with endings such as -ing, -ed, -ly, -er and -est. For example, announced can give announce.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets inflected words match their root in the word list or the source material.
sections.watch_out: Roots are guessed by cutting letters, so a wrong root can match a real word by accident.

sections.name: isOrdinaryEnglish
sections.title: Is this word ordinary English
sections.what: Decides whether a word is ordinary vocabulary by checking the large list, the everyday list, plural and root forms, and the derivational endings. This is the rule that exempts a word from the name check.
sections.why: The comment says it returns true when a word is ordinary English rather than a name.
sections.watch_out: This is the main exemption, so making it too generous lets invented names pass.

sections.name: materialHas
sections.title: Does the material contain this word
sections.what: Checks whether a word appears in the cluster's source material, allowing for plural forms, -ing forms and roots.
sections.why: Rule two in the header: a name found in the material is supported.
sections.watch_out: Matching is by substring, so a short name can match inside a longer word and pass when it should not.

sections.name: Token
sections.title: Shape of one word token
sections.what: Describes one word from the text: the raw text, the letters only form, and whether it starts a sentence.
sections.why: Likely reason: the sentence-start flag is needed for the sentence-start exemption.
sections.watch_out: Digits and other symbols are removed, so a name written with numbers is judged on its letters only.

sections.name: tokenize, hasInternalCaps
sections.title: Split text into words and sentence starts
sections.what: Splits text into words, marks the first word of each sentence, and treats colons, dashes and bullets as sentence breaks. A separate check flags words with a lower-case letter followed by a capital, such as the middle of a joined name.
sections.why: The comment says model rationales use bullets, colons and dashes as sentence breaks.
sections.watch_out: Sentence starts are guessed from punctuation, so a missing full stop makes the next word look like a sentence start and be exempted.

sections.name: findUnsupportedEntity
sections.title: Find the first invented name
sections.what: Scans the name and rationale and returns the first word that looks like an invented entity, or nothing. It skips words under four letters, checks capitalised words and words with internal capitals, and first accepts any word found in the material. Words with internal capitals are always flagged; other words also pass if they are sentence starts or ordinary English.
sections.why: This is the function the guard uses to decide whether a model's name is fabricated.
sections.watch_out: The file header says numbers and web addresses are always checked, but this function has no such check, so they pass here unless checked elsewhere.

summary: Checks entity names written by a model against the source material and rejects names that look invented, while letting ordinary English words through.
purpose: Stop made-up company, place and project names from reaching a finished lessons output.
why: The header comment explains the change: the earlier rule rejected ordinary words, which pushed good names back to plain fallbacks. The rule that an entity name must appear in the material is stated as unchanged.
how: First, split the text into words and mark which words start a sentence. Second, skip words shorter than four letters. Third, accept any word found in the source material, allowing plural and -ing forms. Fourth, reject a word with internal capitals. Fifth, accept a word that starts a sentence. Sixth, accept a word judged to be ordinary English. Last, return the word as a suspected invented name.
inputs: Text fields (a name and a rationale), the source material for the cluster in lower case, and a function that finds word stems.
outputs: The first suspicious word found, or nothing if every word passes.
risks: A real entity whose name is also an ordinary word, such as Shell, passes without a check. The header says numbers and web addresses are always checked, but this function shows no such check. Hyphenated words whose parts are all short can pass without checks. Material matching is by substring, so a short name can match inside a longer word.
debug: If a valid name is rejected, check whether it appears in the source material and whether it has internal capitals. If an invented name passes, check whether it is also an ordinary word, starts a sentence, or appears in the word lists. The English word list is large and central, so changes there change results across the board.
